summary: Reports the outcome of the Internet Architecture Board's workshop on the future of Internet messaging, held on 6 and 7 October 2004 in Burlingame, California. It looked at email, instant messaging, and voice messaging, their commonalities and differences, and topics for future work. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A meeting report about how email, chat, and voice messages are alike and different, and what to work on next.

subtitle: Unified messaging challenges and research directions for email, IM, and voice

tldr.problem: Email, instant messaging, and voice messaging evolved separately with different protocols and capabilities. Users want unified messaging, but the systems have different assumptions about delivery, security, identity, and transport.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reports discussions from the 2004 IAB Messaging Workshop identifying common themes across messaging systems: authorization, multiple channels, negotiation, user control, transport, and identity distribution.
tldr.outcome: The workshop identified research and engineering topics for future work to improve messaging interoperability while recognizing that unified messaging likely requires advances in security, identity, and protocol design.

today: RFC 4417 is an Internet Standard. While unified messaging was not fully achieved, many of its recommendations influenced subsequent work: IMAP extensions for mobile mail, development of presence protocols, reputation system research, and standardization of message filtering rules all built on the workshop's findings. Modern unified communication platforms address many of the workshop's identified challenges.

sections.title: The Messaging Landscape
sections.content:
Traditional email, instant messaging (IM), and voice messaging evolved independently as separate systems with different transports, protocols, and design assumptions. Email is asynchronous and store-and-forward, optimized for multimedia attachments and offline message management. Instant messaging is synchronous and presence-aware, optimized for immediate back-and-forth text exchanges. Voice messaging is real-time for recording but asynchronous for retrieval, optimized for audio quality and low latency.

Yet users want seamless communication across all three media: sending an email that might also notify via IM, receiving a voicemail notification via text message, and transferring a conversation between media types. The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) convened a workshop in October 2004 to examine the current state of messaging technologies, identify commonalities, and suggest directions for future work. This RFC reports the workshop's findings and recommendations.
sections.plainLanguage: Email sits in a mailbox you check later, chat happens right now with someone online, and voicemail is recorded messages you play back. People want all three to work together, but they're built completely differently.

sections.title: Issues Across All Messaging Types
sections.content:
The workshop identified six common themes in messaging systems:

Authorization concerns who can send messages to whom. Traditional email uses block and allow lists, but these are limited—allow lists prevent new contacts, block lists fail because senders can create new identities. The workshop discussed reputation systems where recipients assess sender trustworthiness based on message history, and token-based authorization where recipients grant time-limited permission to send.

Multiple communication channels force users to maintain contact information across phone, email, IM, pager, and other media. Senders don't know the best way to reach someone. Recipients want suppression of redundant messages arriving via different channels. The workshop discussed frameworks for publishing preferred contact methods and for managing delivery rules based on recipient preferences.

Negotiation covers how participants agree on communication parameters: which medium to use (phone call, video conference, chat), who participates, when it occurs, whether it's recorded. This is especially important for multiparty communication.

User control addresses filtering and organizing messages. Users want to organize messages into threads, conversations, and activities (sets of related messages and resources). They want filtering based on sender reputation, content, or other criteria, with the ability to bounce, ignore, file, archive, or forward messages.

Message transport must handle different underlying protocols and media. Some systems tolerate slow links, others require reliability. The workshop discussed fragmenting messages so different parts travel via different transports, with re-assembly at the destination.

Identity and key distribution involve authentication and encryption. The workshop noted that cryptographic key exchange and identity verification are difficult for end users but essential for trust.
sections.plainLanguage: All messaging systems face similar questions: Who can message you? How do you reach someone? What medium to use? How to organize messages? How to keep them secret? How to verify who's really sending?

sections.title: Research and Engineering Recommendations
sections.content:
The workshop separated recommendations into three categories:

Engineering tasks included a distributed reputation service for authorization (needed so recipients can assess unfamiliar senders), a service publishing contact information and capabilities, standards for cross-referencing messages across channels to suppress duplicates, and standardized representation of message filtering rules (extensions to the Sieve mail filtering language).

Architecture tasks included defining threads (ordered sets of messages within a medium), conversations (sets of threads across media), and activities (conversations plus related resources). The workshop also identified a need for conversation identifiers to allow tracking of messages across media. Work was needed on contact publication (how senders discover who someone is and how to reach them) and on frameworks for recipient-defined delivery rules.

Research topics included reputation systems (reactive assessment of trustworthiness), accreditation (proactive assessment by trusted parties), token-based authorization, and multiple-transport delivery where different parts of a message can travel via different media. The workshop also identified research on message synchronization across transports and on partial message retrieval (downloading only selected parts of large attachments).
sections.plainLanguage: New engineering should include: reputation services so you know if a stranger is trustworthy, contact lookup systems, better filtering, and ways to identify conversations across media. Research should explore: trust scoring, time-limited permissions, and splitting messages across different networks.

sections.title: Identity, Transport, and Security Challenges
sections.content:
The workshop identified that identity verification and key distribution are difficult in practice, despite being theoretically well-understood. Getting new root certificates installed, obtaining certificates, and discovering others' public keys remain barriers. However, email, IM, and telephony have similar trust models, which offers opportunity for unified solutions.

Transport presents challenges because different messaging systems use different underlying protocols. Some are push-oriented (IM, where the server sends notifications), others pull-oriented (email, where the client retrieves messages). When fragmenting messages across transports, endpoints must be identified reliably, and the system must handle cases where the same person is reachable via multiple transports at different times. Recovery from transient transport failures and reassembly of message fragments are non-trivial problems.

The workshop noted that identity hints (shared knowledge, conversation style, voice tone, messaging patterns) often provide better verification than cryptographic artifacts for typical users. Nevertheless, a programmatic means for establishing trusted communications between business entities (business-to-business and business-to-customer relationships) would be valuable.
sections.plainLanguage: Proving identity over networks is hard—getting encryption keys installed and distributed is still manual. Messages traveling via different networks need to be reassembled. Humans often recognize senders by their communication style better than by digital signatures.

sections.title: Scope and Out-of-Scope Topics
sections.content:
The workshop notably kept spam (unsolicited bulk email, UCE/UBE) off its agenda despite it being an impetus for the workshop, reasoning that broader authorization and identity issues would cover the architectural problems. Similarly, guaranteed delivery (a fax user's expectation that a fax sent is a fax delivered) was recognized as out of scope for Internet mail work.

The workshop also noted that message queuing systems with guaranteed delivery and transactional integrity (used in enterprise workflows) were operationally out of scope. The focus was on communication between humans using Internet protocols rather than machine-to-machine guaranteed delivery systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop stayed focused: it didn't try to solve spam completely (believing authorization work covers it), didn't promise guaranteed delivery like fax does, and ignored business workflow systems that need absolute reliability.
